subtype: Saying goodbye and taking leave at work [Regulating]
passage: I was in the corridor when I saw Omkar leave the team for the new job. I am Tushar, the one who sits by the printer. At the Friday meeting, Omkar thanked the team by name, said, "This is my last day, and I will finish the handover file by five," and shook a few hands. It was clear and warm. Two weeks before, another colleague had gone silent, just stopped coming and said nothing, and we still do not know what happened. That left everyone uneasy. Omkar sent a note that evening saying, "Thank you all, and my door is open if you need anything." I felt the difference. Warm closure keeps trust.

qa.q: What did Omkar say would be finished by five?
qa.a: Omkar said the handover file would be finished by five.

qa.q: What did the narrator feel about the other colleague's silent exit compared with Omkar's?
qa.a: The narrator felt uneasy about the silent exit, which left everyone unsure what happened, while Omkar's clear thanks and note felt warm.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that kept trust?
qa.a: Omkar thanked people by name, said when the last day was, promised the handover file and left the door open.

qa.q: How might the team have felt after the other colleague went silent?
qa.a: They probably felt uneasy, confused and a bit hurt, since nobody knew what happened.

grounding: Observer's account of a young professional taking leave from a job with thanks, a clear ending and an open door, in contrast with a vague exit.

subtype: Saying goodbye and taking leave at work [Regulating]
passage:
Day 1. Yogesh told his manager at the end of the meeting, "I might leave at some point, maybe." It landed awkwardly. Dhruv, his colleague, felt uneasy and did not know what to plan.

Day 6. Yogesh asked for ten minutes. "I have accepted an offer. My last day will be the 30th. Thank you for what I have learned here. I will document my work and train Dhruv on the client files." Dhruv nodded, relieved to have clarity.

Day 25. At the farewell tea, Yogesh thanked people one by one. "Stay in touch," he said. Dhruv found he meant it, since Yogesh answered a query the next week.

qa.q: What did Yogesh offer to train Dhruv on?
qa.a: Yogesh offered to train Dhruv on the client files.

qa.q: What did Dhruv feel after the vague first comment, and how did that change on day 6?
qa.a: Dhruv felt uneasy and did not know what to plan, but by day 6 the clear news and a date brought relief. Clarity helped more than the news itself.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do that kept trust when leaving?
qa.a: Yogesh gave a clear date, thanked the team, documented the work and stayed in touch.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt at the first vague remark?
qa.a: The manager probably felt uncertain and unable to plan, like Dhruv.

grounding: Before, during and after account of a young professional taking leave with clear thanks, a date and an open door instead of a vague exit.

subtype: Saying goodbye and taking leave at work [Regulating]
passage: Jasleen, you're leaving on Friday, so let me, Naveen, tell you how I left my first job, and then you do the opposite. I was twenty-five, at a small ad agency in Bandra. I'd found a better offer, and I was so nervous about telling my boss, Mrs. Fernandes, that I emailed my resignation at eleven at night, served my notice avoiding her, and on the last day just didn't come back after lunch. No goodbye. No thank you. She had trained me from nothing. Six years later I walked into an interview, and she was on the panel. She was polite. I didn't get the job. Maybe that wasn't why, but I've never forgotten her face. So on Friday, go round. Thank each person for one real thing. Tell your manager you'd be glad to stay in touch. Say goodbye properly, and leave the door open behind you.

qa.q: Where did Naveen work at twenty-five?
qa.a: At a small ad agency in Bandra.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about telling Mrs. Fernandes?
qa.a: Naveen felt nervous and avoidant, so scared of the conversation that the resignation went by late-night email.

qa.q: What turning point made Naveen see the cost of the abrupt exit?
qa.a: Walking into an interview six years later and finding Mrs. Fernandes on the panel, polite but distant, which Naveen never forgot.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Fernandes have felt when Naveen left without a goodbye?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and unappreciated, having trained Naveen from nothing and received no thanks.

grounding: An elder recalls an abrupt exit from a first job damaging a relationship and advises thanks and warm closure when leaving.

subtype: Saying goodbye and taking leave at work [Regulating]
passage: The workshop with Vishal's team had run forty minutes over, and Shalini's flight to Chennai left in two hours. The map on her phone already showed red on the airport road. She could just slip out while Vishal was mid-slide; half the room was on laptops anyway. But she'd seen colleagues do that, and clients always remembered. At the next pause she caught Vishal's eye and raised a hand. "Vishal, I'm so sorry, I have to leave in five minutes for my flight. Can I take one minute now?" He nodded. "Thank you all for today, especially for the honest feedback on the pricing model. I'll send the revised version by Wednesday, and Karan will stay for the rest." At the door she shook Vishal's hand. "Call me any time before Wednesday if something comes up." She made the flight with ten minutes to spare. On Wednesday, Vishal replied within the hour.

qa.q: By when did Shalini promise the revised version?
qa.a: By Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling as the workshop overran?
qa.a: Shalini felt pressured and anxious about the flight and was tempted to slip out, but knew clients remember abrupt exits.

qa.q: What made Shalini's exit a good one?
qa.a: She signalled at a pause, asked for a minute, thanked the room for something specific, named next steps and who would stay, and left the door open for calls.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt if Shalini had slipped out mid-slide?
qa.a: He might have felt slighted and unsure of next steps, remembering it as a careless exit.

grounding: Shows a young professional under time pressure leaving a meeting with thanks, clear next steps and an open door instead of slipping out.

subtype: Saying goodbye and taking leave at work [Regulating]
passage: On her last day at the Kochi design studio, Chandrika had planned to slip out at five with a quick "Bye, all!" in the group chat. Goodbyes made her throat tight. But at lunch she saw Devika, the intern she'd mentored all year, sitting alone and not quite looking at her. Chandrika remembered how she'd felt when her own first mentor vanished without a word. So in the afternoon she went desk to desk. To Rahim: "Thank you for fixing my files at midnight more times than I can count." To the office manager: "Thanks for always saving me a chair." Last, she sat next to Devika. "You've grown so much this year. I'm moving to Bengaluru, not to the moon. Message me whenever you're stuck, and send me your portfolio next month; I'll review it." Devika's face cleared. "Really?" "Really." At five Chandrika left, eyes wet, the door open behind her.

qa.q: Where is Chandrika moving?
qa.a: To Bengaluru.

qa.q: How might Devika have been feeling at lunch?
qa.a: Devika was probably sad and a little hurt, sitting alone and not quite looking at Chandrika, perhaps worried about losing her mentor.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do instead of the quick group message, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She thanked people one by one for specific things and offered Devika ongoing help, which kept trust and left doors open instead of an abrupt exit.

qa.q: What would have changed if Chandrika had only posted 'Bye, all!'?
qa.a: Devika might have felt forgotten, as Chandrika once did with her own mentor, and the relationships might have faded instead of continuing.

grounding: Shows a young professional choosing warm, specific goodbyes and an open door on leaving a job instead of a vague exit.

subtype: Saying goodbye and taking leave at work [Regulating]
passage:
"So this is it," Ankita said, as Ritu packed the last mug into her bag. "Last day."
"Last day. Before I go, can I say something properly?"
"Of course."
"Thank you for the two years. Especially for letting me run the school outreach even when I was new. I learned more from that than anything."
Ankita smiled. "You earned it."
"And the handover notes are in the shared folder. Payal has all the contacts. If anything's unclear, message me, even next month."
"You don't have to do that."
"I want to. I'd like to stay in touch. Coffee once I've settled in?"
"I'd like that." Ankita paused. "You know, the last person who left just stopped coming on a Friday. We found out from the attendance sheet."
Ritu winced. "Ouch."
"Yeah. This is much better. Now go, before I get sentimental."

qa.q: Where are the handover notes?
qa.a: The handover notes are in the shared folder.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as Ritu said goodbye?
qa.a: Ankita felt touched and a little sad to see Ritu go, joking about getting sentimental.

qa.q: Which parts of Ritu's goodbye kept trust strong?
qa.a: Specific thanks, clear handover notes and a contact person, an offer to answer questions later, and a plan to stay in touch.

qa.q: How was the last person's exit different for the team?
qa.a: That person just stopped coming on a Friday and the team found out from the attendance sheet, so it felt abrupt, with no thanks or handover.

grounding: Taking leave from a job with thanks, a clear handover and an open door keeps trust, while an abrupt exit damages it.
